Nov 19th 2026
Donald Trump attended the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit in Shenzhen. He was given a lavish welcome by Xi Jinping, which Mr Trump said “was great respect, and I appreciate that”. He held one-on-one talks with Mr Xi and also with Vladimir Putin before the three men met for trilateral talks, the first ever formal discussions between the leaders of America, Russia and China. Before the APEC summit Mr Trump visited the Association of South-East Asian Nations forum in Manila, where he held a meeting with the leaders of Australia, India and Japan, countries that with America form the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, a forum co-operating on defence and economics to counter China’s growing power in the region.
Before the APEC summit two suspected Russian military aircraft entered Japanese air space near the island of Okinoshima, which is located 80km (50 miles) north of the city of Fukuoka. Japan lodged a formal protest with Moscow, describing the incident as “a serious infringement of Japan’s sovereignty”. Taiwan also reported that it had spotted two Russian planes close to its east coast on two separate occasions.
The International Court of Justice in The Hague ruled that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya people in 2017. The court found that Myanmar’s security forces “perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence as well as acts of extreme violence against children and attacked fleeing Rohingya” in their attempt to drive them out of Rakhine state. International courts have made other determinations of genocide in Rwanda, Srebrenica and Cambodia, but this is the first time a state has been found to have carried out such crimes.
Ukraine mounted another big drone attack on Russian infrastructure and partly destroyed the Kerch bridge , which links Russia to Crimea. The bridge was built by Russia following its annexation of Crimea in 2014. Meanwhile, Jared Kushner, one of Mr Trump’s envoys, said progress was being made in negotiations to end the war. America wants Ukraine’s European allies to be involved in the next stage of talks, but the Kremlin dismissed suggestions that Russia had agreed to their participation. Russia had said earlier the EU needed to choose a representative if it wanted to attend negotiations.
Eight people were arrested in Estonia for an attempted attack on a defence company that develops technology for drones which are supplied to Ukraine. The government said the attack was directed by Russian military intelligence, and in response threatened to shut Estonia’s border with Russia from December 1st.
In Turkey the authorities seized control of the last pro-opposition television station. Prosecutors allege that the owner of Sozcu TV has links to the Gulen movement, which the government blames for an attempted coup in 2016. Lawyers for the station claimed that earlier court cases found no evidence of wrongdoing. Sozcu TV has been reporting on the investigations into a financial scandal that has wiped out the savings of nearly half a million people.
An independent review by Alan Milburn, a former government minister, on working opportunities for young people in Britain proposed a ten-year plan to tackle persistently high disengagement from the workforce. Those not in education, employment or training (NEETs) make up 13% of 16- to 24-year-olds. The review suggests a path to reduce this to 5% by 2036. The government welcomed the report, but many businesses say that recent regulatory changes and tax rises make it too costly to employ young workers.
Andy Burnham declared that Britain lost more than it gained from leaving the European Union, as the prime minister prepared to meet EU leaders for a summit that will discuss closer co-operation on a range of issues. The British are focusing on agreements to reduce red tape in the food-and-drink trade and to align carbon-emissions policy.
Meanwhile, it was announced that Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands will deport illegal migrants to a “return hub” in Rwanda starting next year. EU legislation now allows countries to send migrants to facilities outside Europe. The pilot scheme in Rwanda would apply to migrants who have exhausted all their legal options and are unable to return to their country of origin. Human-rights groups criticised the deal, saying it would finance and legitimise a government responsible for serious abuses.
Members of the Israeli Knesset elected Matan Kahana as speaker. Mr Kahana is a member of the centre-right party led by Gadi Eisenkot , who is trying to form a government. The new speaker takes hardline positions on Israeli settlements and any possibility of a future Palestinian state, but both Jewish and Arab opposition parties voted for him.
America attacked Qeshm Island off Iran’s coast in response to Iranian aggression. Bahrain and Kuwait intercepted several aerial attacks; Iran said it was targeting American air-defence systems and the Ali al-Salem air base in Kuwait, where America maintains a presence. Iran made several claims of tankers hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
Pro-government forces in Yemen announced their withdrawal from territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab, a vital waterway into the Red Sea. The forces are backed by Saudi Arabia and are shifting their troops to reinforce positions around Aden, the interim capital, as fighting intensifies against the Houthis, Iranian-backed rebels. The Houthis have ramped up attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure.
South Sudan again postponed elections, from December 22nd to February 11th, ostensibly to give authorities more time to register voters. Armed conflict has intensified since the collapse of a power-sharing deal last year between Salva Kiir, the president, and Riek Machar, his main rival and former vice-president, who has been charged with treason and put under house arrest. A legitimate election looks far off.
Pete Hegseth, America’s secretary of war, visited Venezuela, where he announced a pact to co-operate on military and security matters, covering training and intelligence. Mr Hegseth warned drug traffickers that “Your ​time is up. We will hunt you down.” At least 240 people have been killed in America’s controversial policy of conducting strikes on suspected drug-running boats.
A journalist who investigated possible links between drug-traffickers and politicians in Costa Rica was shot dead. It is the first known assassination in 25 years of a journalist in Costa Rica, which is relatively peaceful compared with its neighbours, though drug violence is on the rise.
In Haiti Martine Moïse, the widow of Jovenel Moïse, the former president who was assassinated in 2021, registered as a candidate in the presidential election due to be held next July. The election has been long delayed, and could be again if security forces cannot control gang violence. Haiti’s security minister credited the deployment of troops from El Salvador with helping to curb the trouble, before meeting the Salvadoran president, Nayib Bukele, for talks about extending the deployment.
Two weeks after the midterm elections, Mary Peltola was declared the winner in Alaska’s Senate race. Her victory means the Democrats will hold 56 seats in the Senate when it convenes in January, to the Republicans’ 44. After spending close to $500m on Republican campaigns in the midterms Elon Musk now says he feels “pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it”.

Nov 19th 2026
Investors took some comfort from Nvidia’s latest quarterly earnings , which recorded $116bn in revenue, up by 103% year on year. The company also raised its sales forecast. The results were presented by Colette Kress, who was appointed interim chief executive after the resignation of Jensen Huang for having affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and two subordinates. “I own my mistakes completely,” Mr Huang conceded, though he suggested he wanted to return as CEO. The board said it had no intention of reinstating him. Its investigation into Mr Huang’s conduct continues. It has also created a committee to oversee national security and exports.
Mr Huang’s departure continued to unsettle markets. Attention turned to efforts by Congress to close, by the end of the year, loopholes that have allowed advanced AI chips to end up in China. The woman at the centre of the Huang affair worked for Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm suspected of smuggling Nvidia’s chips. America’s Commerce Department issued new restrictions on exports of advanced chips to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. It aims to stop Chinese firms obtaining the chips through those countries.
The fallout spread to Donald Trump’s cabinet, when Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, chastised the Commerce Department , led by Howard Lutnick, for not banning exports to Megaspeed. Democrats in Congress are reportedly looking into allegations that the department’s decisions may have been influenced by Mr Lutnick’s ties to Cantor Fitzgerald, an investment firm. The department said Mr Lutnick had fully complied with ethics agreements and divested all financial interests in Cantor.
Responding to huge demand for its stock, Anthropic priced the shares in its IPO at $83, above the price it had previously laid out to investors, valuing the company at $1.5trn. The IPO raised a total of $107bn (including the private placement), making it the biggest ever, before the stock began trading on November 19th.
ICEYE, a Finnish satellite-imaging company, offered to buy Avio, an Italian rocket-maker, for around €2.1bn ($2.3bn). ICEYE said the deal was intended to produce a vertically integrated space and defence company. Rows over restrictions on the Starlink and Starshield services in Ukraine, which are provided by SpaceX, have made Europe keen to beef up its domestic space industry.
SpaceX’s ambition to develop fully and rapidly reusable rockets came a big step closer when the returning upper stage of its Starship rocket was caught by mechanical arms at the launch site for the first time. SpaceX has caught Starship’s booster before (though an attempt to capture the booster failed this time). Getting Starship fully operational is vital to the company’s plan to expand its Starlink satellite-broadband service and to put AI data-centres into space.
The years of waiting were at last over for gaming fans, as “ Grand Theft Auto VI ”, described as the most anticipated video game ever, was finally released. It has been over 13 years since the previous title in the GTA series was published.
A cost-cutting exercise at Disney is expected to generate $3bn in savings, the company said. It intends to reinvest that money in providing more content for its streaming platforms, tailored especially for its faster-growing markets outside America.
GDP in Japan unexpectedly shrank by 0.1% in the third quarter at an annualised rate. Comparatively high inflation has caused Japanese consumers to tighten their belts, leading to a decline in private consumption, which accounts for roughly half of output. Energy costs remain high and import prices have risen because of the weak yen.
Indonesia’s central bank increased interest rates. The bank has been battling all year to defend the rupiah, which has come under pressure from concerns about Indonesia’s public spending and fiscal transparency. The country’s stock market plunged in October when MSCI said it was dysfunctional and threatened to downgrade Indonesia’s emerging-market status.
The annual rate of inflation in Britain nudged up again in October, to 3.6%. The average price of petrol was at its highest level since August 2022.
The Trump administration asked Congress for $50bn to fix outdated air-traffic control systems after thousands of flights were grounded across America; legacy equipment had become unstable after being flooded with data. Around the same time Microsoft’s office software and communications platforms went offline. And customers at several banks reported access issues. There was no evidence of foul play in the cluster of glitches, but that didn’t stop speculation swirling of a global technological meltdown. Reports suggested that some consumers were panic-buying; Costco was said to have sold out of generators.

In February 1945 Winston Churchill, Franklin Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin met in Yalta to decide the planet’s future. As their armies pressed for victory against Nazi Germany, the leaders of Britain, America and the Soviet Union carved up Europe into what became communist and capitalist blocs. Historians differ as to whether the Allies could have struck a better deal, but no one doubts that the meeting was historic. Unlike this week’s photo opportunity in Shenzhen for Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Described by some as the new Yalta, it is nothing of the sort. President Trump, fresh from humiliation in the midterms, wants to look strong again on television. Russia’s despot, humiliated by years of failure to conquer his smaller neighbour, wants to rub shoulders with real superpowers. China’s leader is happy to appear as the gracious emperor welcoming squabbling foreigners to his villa . But little of substance is likely to emerge. Mr Trump's technique of winging it will not sway the tightly scripted Mr Xi.
The real story in geopolitics is the deepening collaboration between four autocratic, anti-Western regimes: China, Russia, Iran and North Korea . This is not new: Mr Trump’s first defence secretary identified the threat in 2018. It is not a formal alliance, either, and its members are very different. China is an economic and technological colossus, as the dancing robots and ubiquitous delivery drones of Shenzhen make clear. Russia’s is a middling economy; Iran and North Korea are midgets. Iran is a theocracy; China and North Korea are godless, unless you count Kim Jong Un. In Beijing, Moscow and Pyongyang, one man rules; in Tehran it is unclear who does . But all four regimes share a core interest: they want a world safe for autocrats, specifically themselves. And as Mr Trump weakens America’s wider and deeper network of alliances, America’s foes are quietly helping each other.
The most obvious collusion is military. When Russia ravages Ukrainian cities, it does so with Iranian drone technology and Chinese components. Iranian engineers study how Russia fine-tunes their murderous designs. North Korea has sent some 16,000 soldiers to fight and die for Mr Putin, in return for cash and military technology. China stops short of direct military aid, but is soaking up data on how Russian drones perform in combat—handy for a superpower that has not fought a serious war since 1979. Meanwhile, the missiles Iran aims at American forces in the Gulf can be fired quickly (thanks to Chinese precursor chemicals for solid fuel) and accurately (thanks to Russian intelligence and Chinese satellite data).
Economic collaboration is deepening, too. Trade with China keeps the other three economies afloat. Chinese payments systems offer ways to dodge Western sanctions. More than 95% of Russia’s trade with China is now in yuan or roubles, up from around 25% five years ago. Russian oil flows to China and North Korea; Iranian oil is shipped to China, largely via a “shadow fleet” of sanctions-busting ships that has grown by 1,500% since 2022. North Korean workers toil in Russian factories, easing the labour shortage caused by Mr Putin sending so many Russians to their deaths in Ukraine.
Axis diplomats scratch one another’s backs. They vote in harmony at the UN, where Russian and Chinese vetoes block any serious moves to restrain Mr Putin’s wars. Axis propagandists amplify one another’s narratives on screens everywhere, and promote stories that undermine Western democracies.
Those who doubt the importance of the axis of malice note that the interests of its constituent regimes often fail to align. Iran, North Korea and Russia are rogue states; China is far more cautious. Having prospered hugely from globalisation, it does not want the American-led rules-based order to be replaced by chaos. It has long frowned on North Korea’s destabilisation of its backyard. And unlike oil-producing Russia, it suffers when Iran’s war with America drives up oil prices.
Yet although they do not always pull in the same direction, these four regimes increasingly find ways to benefit from their shared antagonism towards America. China can cope with the irritation of costly oil, and sees great advantage if American aircraft-carriers are stuck in the Gulf instead of patrolling the Pacific. It does not want Mr Putin to start a wider war in Europe—Europeans are valuable customers for Chinese goods—but it is happy to see the West bogged down defending Ukraine with resources that might otherwise go to support Taiwan. And as Mr Putin deepens his ties with Kim Jong Un, China is less inclined to scold North Korea for its nuclear troublemaking; Mr Kim is adept at playing one friend off against another.
There are precedents for informal collusion between geographically dispersed and culturally disparate authoritarian regimes. The most alarming is the original axis in the 1930s. Fascist Germany, Italy and Japan did not love one another, but they all felt aggrieved by the dominant powers. Germany and Japan did not fight arm in arm, but by expanding their empires at the same time, they offered the West two huge challenges at once, thus improving their own chances of victory. Today, if China decides to invade Taiwan, there is a good chance that Russia, Iran or North Korea will provoke a simultaneous crisis elsewhere, or in cyberspace.
This analogy goes only so far. Mr Putin, despite the hundreds of thousands of deaths he has caused, is not Hitler. But it would be rash for today’s democracies to ignore the threat posed by the axis of malice. Their systems of government seem unlikely to change soon. (Their citizens do not get a say.) With each passing day, their hackers have access to more powerful AI tools, and it is uncertain whether the West’s defences will keep up. Authoritarian systems are not as good as liberal democracies at generating wealth, fostering innovation or allowing their people decent lives. But when they collude, they can make the world darker and more dangerous. Democracies must recognise the peril in order to confront it. ■

Britain’s armed forces are in a tight spot. Cash is short; danger is not. Iranian threats against British air bases, made credible by cheap attack drones, are becoming routine. Russian naval activity around the country’s waters has risen by 40% over the past year. America demands that Europe pay for its own security, and is backing away from commitments to defend it. Former army chiefs warn that Britain is ill-prepared for conflict. Its only truly successful living naval commander, James Bond , is fictitious.
The good news is that necessity is the mother of invention. The Royal Navy is placing a huge, risky bet on a futuristic new fleet: a “hybrid navy” mixing crewed, uncrewed and autonomous vessels, integrated in part by AI. Much of the technology is unproven and the bet could backfire. Yet the navy is going all in, because it believes it has no choice. If it succeeds, it will transform the nature of sea power .
Britain’s navy has two big jobs which are essential for the security of its European allies and NATO. The first is keeping submarine-mounted nuclear missiles at sea at all times to deter attacks. The second is protecting communication lines and infrastructure in the North Atlantic and High North. These would be crucial in a war, especially with Russia, which is pouring resources into its northern fleet.
Partly because of the first job’s vast cost (a quarter of Britain’s defence budget), the navy thinks it may fail in the second unless it shakes things up. The fundamental idea behind the hybrid navy is to split up the functions of the exquisite, enormously expensive warships it now relies on. These will instead be spread over many smaller, nimbler, cheaper ships performing specialised roles. The “Common Combat Vessels” that will act as command centres for these fleets should cost £200m ($260m) each, compared with about five times that for a high-end frigate and over £2.5bn for an air-defence destroyer.
The new fleets promise to control the seas far more efficiently than existing ones. With more hulls they can cover a greater area than a smaller number of warships. Vessels will be much bigger and more sophisticated than the one-way attack ships used to great effect by Ukraine in the Black Sea. But they will be able to take more risk than traditional ones, being both cheaper and often uncrewed.
Since the hybrid navy’s vessels should be simpler to build, more commercial shipyards will compete to do so. That will help control costs. It also carries echoes of NASA’s decision, in the 2000s, to welcome startups into its rocket programme. That policy helped spawn SpaceX, one of the world’s biggest firms, and handed America a gigantic lead in space warfare.
However, getting the hybrid navy afloat will involve daunting risks. Naval drones tend to have less endurance and armament than larger, crewed warships. Also, Britain’s sea forces do not work in isolation. Securing the North Atlantic and High North will take close co-operation with America, France and Norway. These allies will need to plug seamlessly into the hybrid navy’s new operating system.
Mistakes are inevitable: no country has tried this before. Some may arise from the new doctrinal questions hybrid fleets pose. If Russia attacked a crewed warship, Britain would see it as an act of war. What about an uncrewed one? The navy must learn from the mistakes it will make, and fast.
Moreover, without enough money the project will sink. Britain’s sailors have clocked that a radical new idea is a good way to grab cash from a limited pot. Launching the hybrid navy will still take perhaps another £32bn by 2035—about half of this year’s defence budget. The government has yet to say how it will fund such investments. Even so, huzzah for the Royal Navy. Too often, Britain balks at risk and so commits itself to stagnation. Its navy is doing the opposite. ■

Somehow, try to move on from Jensen Huang. The leather-jacketed ex-boss of the chip designer Nvidia , who was turfed out after two (alleged) affairs with subordinates and one (admitted) dalliance with an (alleged) Chinese agent, is eyeing a comeback. Yet, captivating as Mr Huang’s manoeuvres are, the fracas at Nvidia has underscored a deeper, and more consequential tale: China’s hell-for-leather scramble to gain access to the technology behind American artificial intelligence, by whatever means necessary.
Smuggling chips into China is only the start. Probably more important has been remote access to data centres, mainly in South-East Asia. It offered a sometimes-legal route for Chinese developers to train their models with top-end chips—until November 16th, when America’s Bureau of Industry and Security, the branch of the Commerce Department that runs chip controls, set out a rule restricting the practice. Remote access and smuggling together roughly doubled the compute, or processing power, available to Chinese AI companies from domestic production and legal imports alone, estimates the Institute for Progress, a think-tank.
But China wants more than just to get the best chips. It also wishes to build them itself. Behind the rapid growth of China’s domestic semiconductor industry have been campaigns of talent-poaching and industrial espionage, especially focused on researchers in Taiwan and South Korea. CXMT, a Chinese memory giant, was jump-started by former Samsung staff who, South Korean authorities found, left in 2016 with hand-copied notebooks full of production techniques. South Korea jailed a senior defector in April. Top of China’s shopping list and still, tantalisingly, out of reach is extreme-ultraviolet lithography (EUV) technology, which is needed to produce today’s whizziest chips at scale. Only one company in the world, ASML, can produce an EUV machine. The Dutch government, under American pressure, has stopped it from ever exporting one to China.
The staggering breadth of China’s campaign means America must respond forcefully. Not with a crude protectionist purpose, or to hamper Chinese industry broadly, but to ensure an authoritarian regime does not take the lead on AI, let alone win the race to superintelligence. The technology has serious military applications, as the battlefields of Ukraine show. And the closer to the frontier China gets, the harder it will be for America to slow down AI research, making it more likely that the technology brings about disasters.
So far, America’s efforts have been chaotic and confused. That is in part because the Trump administration is divided. The Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, who is cosy with Nvidia, has been astonishingly lax. Rightly, the Huang affair has imperilled Mr Lutnick’s job. Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, used his first television interview after the midterm elections to blame Mr Lutnick for slow-walking restrictions. The instability of policy has frustrated chip companies, which operate in a capital-intensive industry where products and facilities take years to develop.
What now? America is at last cracking down on Chinese firms’ access to overseas data centres, although allowing some access through trusted providers with a kill-switch would offer more leverage than a simple shutdown. More could be done, such as requiring makers of cutting-edge chips to embed location trackers. Broadly, a reasonable standard would be only to allow chips at least two generations old into China (an “n-2” rule), targeting the tech most useful for training frontier AI. America must also work better with allies to tackle Chinese industrial espionage. Hearteningly, Congress is pushing to legislate on these issues.
America cannot halt China’s chipmaking progress. DeepSeek, a Chinese AI champion, says its upcoming model will be pre-trained on domestically produced chips. But merely slowing Chinese AI down is worthwhile and achievable. The industry reckons that China is still ten-plus years away from a commercially viable EUV machine, for instance.
Those years may matter enormously. Recently the mood in Silicon Valley has darkened. A growing share of AI researchers see months, years at most, until AI reliably surpasses humans—including at AI research itself. That might open the door to “recursive self-improvement”, where each model autonomously builds its own successor.
If they are right, the next few years will be tumultuous. Governments in America and elsewhere might have to scramble to contain runaway AI systems while the technology disrupts the economy and society. The task would be daunting. With China threatening to overtake America, it might be impossible. ■

AMERICAN SCIENCE leads the world because of both its home-grown strength and its openness to collaborating with foreigners. The Trump administration prefers to rely only on the first half of the formula. As we exclusively report , the number of grants made by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) involving collaborators abroad has been 38% lower on average in 2025 and 2026 than in 2022-24. At the same time the administration is making it far harder for foreign scientists to study and work in America.
The funding of overseas research needed more oversight. Yet in its approach to foreign know-how and foreign brains, the administration has overcorrected. The results will be bad for humanity, because no other country can advance the frontiers of science as much as an outward-looking America can. They will also be bad for America itself.
The NIH has funded foreign scientists since 1947. In 1960 the International Health Research Act formalised the practice. Its champion, John Fogarty, thought co-operation in medical research would foster peace. That is debatable, but the funding has done enormous good. The NIH’s Fogarty International Centre has trained thousands of health researchers in poorer countries; some alumni now run national health systems. Americans have benefited directly, too. For example, in 2021 an NIH-backed trial showed how to cure TB in four months rather than six. Trials are often faster and cheaper abroad. Enrolling patients is easier for conditions that are more common in other parts of the world, such as HIV.
The Trump administration argues that overseas research can pose a national-security risk and that American taxpayers deserve better oversight. Those are reasonable concerns. The Wuhan Institute of Virology, one possible source of the covid-19 virus, received NIH money through its collaboration with the EcoHealth Alliance, a now-defunct American non-profit. Yet the administration’s approach to reform has been inept and indiscriminate, cutting off money for promising global research on arthritis, hiv, dementia and more. Our analysis suggests the administration’s political preoccupations have played a troubling role in the allocation of cash: research involving South Africa, with which Trumpworld has a beef about race politics, has suffered disproportionately.
The damage to global science and America’s status at its summit is being aggravated by new immigration policies. Visa delays, travel bans and threats to post-study work rights have contributed to a fall of 21% in applications from international students to PhD programmes across 55 of America’s research universities. (New enrolments of other foreign students have also fallen dramatically.) In July a rule was finalised limiting student and exchange visas to four years, shorter than most PhD programmes, after which visa holders must apply for an extension (though this has since been blocked by a court). The Trump administration has proposed charging universities up to $100,000 per student for work authorisation for up to three years after graduation—a prohibitive sum.
Deterring talented foreign scientists from coming to study and work in America is an act of senseless self-harm. Foreigners are not on the margins of science in America. A third of American Nobel laureates in the sciences were born abroad. In 2023 roughly three-fifths of postdoctoral scientists held temporary visas. In Massachusetts, the de facto capital of America’s biotech industry, some 30% of STEM workers were born outside the country. America’s scientific engine would be far weaker without them.
The Republican-controlled Congress has already pushed back against the White House, rejecting a proposed 40% cut to the NIH and refusing to abolish the Fogarty International Centre. The Democrats who will soon take over Congress should stiffen this defence and hold hearings to scrutinise the administration’s actions. So far, science does not feature much in their plans, raising the chances that its neglect will outlast Donald Trump’s presidency. Trust across international research networks takes years to build. So does a reputation for welcoming talented foreigners. There is no time to lose. ■

It would be seen as a giant, were it not bordered on three sides by India. With 180m people, Bangladesh is far more populous than any European country. And on November 24th its multitudes were supposed to achieve a new status. No longer was their country to be classed as “least-developed”, a UN category that allows poor nations cheap development loans and low-tariff access to rich markets.
Bangladeshis were ready to celebrate. Sure, shirt- and skirt-exporters would lose an edge. But rising in this global league table would be a point of pride for a country that has much to be proud of. Bangladesh was born bloodily in 1971, when the former East Pakistan split from what was then called West Pakistan after a vile war. At the time, it was the second-poorest country in the world. Since then it has quadrupled its income per head, slashed child mortality, educated nearly all of its children and become the world’s largest source of clothes after China.
But the party was postponed. Although Bangladesh has earned promotion, it asked the UN for a three-year deferment, which was granted last month. Sadly, it needs the breathing space. After decades of progress it is suffering an economic crisis.
Part of the blame lies with the thuggish regime of Sheikh Hasina Wajed, which was toppled in a student-led “Gen Z revolution” in 2024. It was replaced by an interim government and then, since February, by the Bangladesh Nationalist Party, the victor in an election from which Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League was barred. Before the revolution, Sheikh Hasina’s cronies looted Bangladesh’s banks, leaving them saddled with bad assets that add up to a third of the total loan book.
Sheikh Hasina fled to India in 2024. But officials say her Awami League is behind strikes in the crucial garment industry and a campaign of crude bombs and arson. The League has reserves of ill-gotten cash and street fighters to draw on. If Sheikh Hasina comes back from exile, the chaos could intensify. Despite having been sentenced to death in absentia for her part in a violent crackdown on protesters before she was toppled, she has vowed to return in December.
Not all problems can be laid at Sheikh Hasina’s door. Some come from outside Bangladesh. Many factories were forced to close this year as the war in Iran disrupted fuel supplies from the Gulf. Costlier fuel spurred workers to demand higher wages, just as factory owners were least able to afford them; hence the strikes. The new government has been slow to grapple with inflation or corruption, and ham-fisted with protesters.
Bangladesh risks an extended period of stagflation. Inflation has been over 8% since the middle of 2022, when it spiked following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which also put up energy prices. Growth in GDP is languishing around the levels seen during the covid-19 pandemic, at 3.5% in 2025, down from around 6%. Poverty is rising for the first time in decades, threatening to undo some of the country’s amazing progress. Inflation has outpaced wage growth for nearly five years. A shortage of good jobs, the original grievance of the student protesters, persists.
A balance-of-payments crisis is unlikely. Payments to foreign creditors, though increasing, will remain small relative to foreign earnings from remittances and garment exports. The problem, rather, is a weakening domestic economy. Debt-service costs may reach 3% of GDP this year, straining public finances. Bangladesh collects only around 7% of GDP in tax. The most urgent priority is to fix Bangladesh’s banks. But if external creditors such as the IMF are to help the government bail them out, they are likely to want the government to rein in costly and distortive subsidies. That will be deeply unpopular.
Bangladesh needs to use its three-year pause to push ahead with reforms that will help it stand on its own two feet. The government needs to boost its tax take. And it should be working hard to sign trade deals to replace preferential access, just as its neighbour India is. Escaping from extreme poverty and ousting a nasty regime is just the start. ■

“ Back to the bench ” (October 24th) reported on America’s new era of private science. You noted the concerns about the present system of government-funded research, where the few committees that steer basic-research grants can lead to groupthink. I share that concern, but I also think that private control is no cure. In mining engineering, and I suspect elsewhere, university researchers increasingly compete with consulting firms for the money that industry supplies to tackle operational problems. But how many of those problems result from a failure to understand the mechanisms governing complex engineering systems, the very thing that basic research tackles? Some have also learned that controlling key conferences, and the papers they generate, is an effective launching pad for guidelines that persuade businesses to buy their services.
Dig deeper, as an academic is supposed to do, and this private work often cannot be reproduced because it rests on confidential documents. Ask to check their methods and results, and the reply is that the data are proprietary. Private science risks becoming closed to scrutiny and, consequently, an instrument for selling products and services rather than a means of discovery.

MORE THAN half of the world’s 18- to 24-year-olds now say that social media and chatbots are their main way to access news. For younger teenagers that number is even higher. Ofcom, Britain’s communications regulator, found that 78% of the country’s 12- to 15-year-olds get their news this way. Adults, too, are shifting their habits, but more slowly.
For young people the change is profound. Previously teenagers had to actively seek out news; now it finds them. Even in the past few years things have shifted as social media has moved from participatory networks to algorithmic discovery. A lot of news is inserted into feeds without being sought.
This naturally leads to concern about misinformation, and it is an issue. Algorithms reinforce opinions or, worse, push views held by company owners. A recent study, published in Nature, randomised American users of Elon Musk’s X so that half saw the algorithmic “for you” feed and half a chronological one of people they followed. The first group were 5.5% likelier to view investigations into Donald Trump as unacceptable.
But news consumers have always been subject to biases. A pensioner reading a partisan newspaper every day is also being fed misinformation, albeit by a human editor rather than an algorithm. If anything, young people are savvier than older ones about the reliability of online content.
The bigger issue is that children are seeing a lot more news than they used to and it is unfiltered. Videos on all sorts of topics flash by in a muddle without context or explanation.
This content also increasingly diverges from what older adults might be seeing on the BBC, or on their more sedate social-media feeds. It is, for instance, typically much less focused on domestic news, with a strong bias towards America, where many content creators live. Your average 16-year-old in Britain is more likely to understand a Zohran Mamdani meme than to know that John Healey is the British chancellor.
For teachers around the world this is a new and difficult challenge. They are used to helping students gradually build up a picture of the world through the controlled delivery of knowledge. Now they are confronted with pupils drinking from a firehose of information and struggling to contextualise any of it.
I am currently chairing a commission for The Economist Educational Foundation with the aim of supporting schools to manage this new world. We have done a lot of polling and focus groups with young people and teachers in Britain, and there is no doubt that it is a problem. At one school, a group of 11-year-old girls told us the big news story in their feeds that week was a contentious case of alleged rape at Cornell, an American university, something that did not feature much in the mainstream British media. The boys in the class had not heard about it—an indication of the kind of information divides that algorithms can create.
Our polling found teachers are worried about how to deal with this. One challenge is simply a lack of resources. Another is a lack of confidence in discussing controversial and divisive issues such as Israel’s occupation of Gaza or race riots. One head teacher, in an area where a lot of St George’s flags were put up on lampposts in the summer of 2025, talked about how difficult it was to discuss this issue with concerned students when parents of other children had been involved in putting the flags up.
When schools do venture into current affairs they tend to avoid these areas of controversy, but it is important to be able to talk about them—not least to help young people work out how to disagree in more constructive ways than their elders. This is something social media actively discourages by incentivising polarising language. Another study of X found that highly negative posts about political opponents significantly outperform positive ones about allies. Increasingly, people say they are less likely to be friends with people who hold a different view.
Counteracting this in a classroom, while dealing with sensitive issues, is a skill that requires training—something The Economist Educational Foundation is working on. At the moment learning how to manage these kinds of conversation, which increasingly occur spontaneously in lessons, is not a formal part of teacher-training courses. It also requires time. The new curriculum in England, due to be taught from September 2028, gives more importance to citizenship and will make it a compulsory subject at primary school, which will help. But conversations also need to be woven into other relevant subjects.
One uncertainty is the impact of social-media bans for children. Britain’s ban, on use by under-16s, is set to come in next year. This will limit access, but it might worsen the information environment as some will find ways of gaining access while others don’t. Scraps of footage being shared on WhatsApp groups will have even less context.
Either way there will be no return to the old model. Teenagers aren’t suddenly going to start reading physical newspapers or watching the evening news. A core purpose of education is to give young people the knowledge they need to be active citizens. It is no longer possible to do that without tackling the very different ways they now see the world. ■
Sam Freedman is a senior fellow at the Institute for Government, a senior adviser to Ark Schools and chair of the Current Affairs Education Commission.
The Economist Educational Foundation is an independent charity that helps children acquire the knowledge and skills they need to navigate complex social and environmental challenges, misinformation and polarisation. economistfoundation.org

ON OCTOBER 29TH TraderTraitor, a state-sponsored North Korean hacking group, stole $6.3bn from Binance, a cryptocurrency exchange. The heist was the largest on record , surpassing the group’s $1.5bn raid on Bybit, another crypto exchange, in 2025. Last week the FBI announced that another North Korean scheme nabbed $400m of cryptocurrency over 18 months, using fake video calls to hijack people’s identities.
Over the past two decades, hostile states have steadily turned their espionage and sabotage efforts away from governments and towards Western businesses, recognising that the innovations of high-tech companies were a source of strategic advantage, and that those companies’ defences fell well short of the value of what they held.
North Korea now treats ordinary commercial activity as a revenue stream. Cut off from the international financial system by sanctions, it makes money in three ways: stealing cryptocurrency, getting workers into Western companies under false identities, and running trading and front companies abroad to move the funds. These often blur into each other, with the same networks doing all three.
For most chief executives, security still means the firewall. That is only half the job. The other half is knowing who is approaching your engineers, who your new hires really are and who is behind the staffing agency or supplier you pay each month. Those questions reach every boardroom, well beyond crypto exchanges and tech firms, and no sanctions list will answer them.
Recruitment has become a front line in this war. At Binance the way in was a job offer to one of its employees: a friendly recruiter, a couple of convincing video interviews and a coding test that carried malicious software into the organisation. Nothing about it looked unusual; this is how millions of people find jobs every year.
It works in reverse, too: companies need to be aware of whom they are really hiring. Many North Korean workers are deployed by the state across industries such as IT, restaurants, medical clinics and building sites. They operate under close surveillance and are made to send their wages home, so a company that hires one is not only putting its data at risk, but helping to fund North Korea’s regime. Shockingly, the hiring checks and sanctions screening that American and European boardrooms rely on would wave the bulk of North Korea’s agents straight through.
Employees are not the only risk. Many companies are also often unaware that by using the wrong supplier or making the wrong payment they could unwittingly be sending money to Pyongyang.
Firms like mine now use agentic AI to trace who owns and deals with whom across thousands of organisations, combing through more public records than any compliance team could check by hand. Using these techniques, Strider has flagged 875 businesses outside North Korea that are linked to dealings with the regime that may break international sanctions. Less than 3% of them are on any government sanctions list or export blacklist. In practice, a business could sign a contract, hire through an agency or pay a supplier linked to North Korea, and its sanctions checks would raise no alarm.
It is unsurprising that 408 of these organisations are based in China and Russia, North Korea’s closest partners. What is surprising is that the rest are spread across more than 70 countries. Eighty-eight are in Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia or the United Arab Emirates, financial centres that Western trade and money pass through every day. North Korea might be shut out of the world economy, but it has found a back door.
Crucially, these are not just companies that exist on paper. More than 300 are flagged as employing North Korean workers abroad, a practice banned by the UN in 2017. Seventy-nine are flagged as having bought or sold North Korean military goods. These shells and missiles are now being fired at Ukrainian cities.
Money linked to Kim Jong Un’s regime can pass through respectable institutions, often without them knowing. A supplier or recruitment agency can look entirely above board, carry all the right paperwork and pass every standard check while being one or two steps removed from a network working on North Korea’s behalf. A sanctions list records only those networks that governments have formally designated, so it shows the threat as it stood on the day each name was added. The networks behind those names are shifting far faster than most governments can update a list.
Shutting out international talent or treating every overseas firm with suspicion would be unrealistic. The aim should be to make openness more secure. In practice, that means three things. First, rigorous due diligence, actively focused on state risks: look past the name on the contract to a partner’s ownership, funding and links to state bodies, before signing rather than after. Second, put that intelligence in front of decision-makers at the point of decision, whether in hiring, procurement or an investment committee. Third, give someone real authority: a C-suite executive with responsibility for enabling the right deals and halting those where the risks are evident, or too opaque.
The biggest theft in crypto history began with a job offer. For decades, economic security was left to governments; North Korea has made it a boardroom problem. Every hire, every supplier and every payment is now a potential way in for a hostile state, and Kim Jong Un’s techno-stooges have shown it needs only one. ■
Greg Levesque is the chief executive and co-founder of Strider Technologies.

To enforce the pledge, his administration maintained rules restricting sales of certain types of semiconductor. Anything less, a Republican congressmen said, would be as foolhardy as handing Iran weapons-grade uranium.
Yet all the while, it turns out, a torrent of Nvidia’s nattiest chips was flowing to China or to middlemen who made them available to Chinese AI firms. INDIA’S 53M HECTARES of rice paddy are picturesque and bountiful. Last year they produced 154m tonnes of rice, 28% of the global total, overtaking China and making India for the first time the world’s largest producer. When paddy fields flood, the soil is starved of oxygen, letting anaerobic organisms called methanogens thrive. The bugs gobble up plant detritus and manure, converting it into energy with methane as a by-product. Rice paddies produce 8-12% of global methane emissions each year. India’s are responsible for 16.5% of that, second only to China’s.
Reducing methane emissions is a good way to slow the pace of global warming. Tonne for tonne, methane is a far more powerful warming gas than carbon dioxide, and it degrades rapidly in the atmosphere, disappearing in around 12 years. So cutting methane emissions can quickly slow the pile-up of greenhouse gases. Carbon dioxide, by contrast, stays aloft for anything from centuries to millennia, which is why climate wonks argue that it should be actively taken out of the atmosphere.
In many countries, particularly heavily industrialised ones, cutting methane emissions mostly means plugging leaks in fossil-fuel infrastructure—good for producers and the atmosphere alike. In India, just under half of methane emissions come from agricultural activities, primarily rice and cattle farming. That creates special challenges for reducing them.
Various approaches are being tried. The solution for rice paddies largely involves using less water for irrigation. Alternate wetting and drying, for instance, means periodically draining the paddies. That lowers water use by roughly a third and also inhibits the methanogens by allowing oxygen into the soil. Studies suggest that as a result emissions can drop by between 30% and 70%. Another method is to use varieties of rice that can be directly seeded in dry soil, rather than being germinated in nurseries and then transplanted into flooded paddies. This saves labour as well as water, and can reduce methane emissions by anything from 30% to 98%.
The picture for livestock is different. Cattle foster methanogens in their stomachs’ first chamber, where they help to break down grass and other food; and India is home to nearly 200m cattle, more than anywhere else except Brazil. The burps from those cows and buffalo account for roughly one-third of India’s agricultural methane emissions.
Mixing more digestible green feeds in with dry fodder reduces the methane load in the burps. Additives can have the same result. Seaweed can reduce methane by 30-80%. The supplement is thought to inhibit an enzyme that the methanogens use to produce methane. Microbes in manure generate methane when it is wet or moist; to reduce these emissions it can be spread out in the sun and left to dry.
Unfortunately, none of this appears to be a priority. India’s climate targets do not single out methane reduction; nor did the government sign up to a 2021 pledge to cut emissions by at least 30% below 2020 levels by 2030. Moreover, much of Indian agriculture is on small-scale subsistence farms, so proposals to change the way they have operated for generations are hard to implement. For low-emissions programmes to take off, they need to give farmers clear incentives, in the shape of increased yields or lower labour or water costs.

India’s farmers need to adjust their practices, and not just to adapt better to the changing climate. Dairy cattle are numerous, but they produce less milk per head than cattle elsewhere. And the country is producing more rice than it can consume, store for food security or export. The government is keen for its farmers to diversify. For smallholders and subsistence farmers who operate season by season, however, making such changes will not seem worthwhile without more protection against failure. ■

It had been among the world’s largest lakes, on which tens of millions of people depended in Chad, Cameroon, Niger and Nigeria, the four countries that share it. First, much of Africa may turn out to be wetter than many expect, especially those who recall the Sahelian droughts of the 1970s and 1980s. Second, exactly how climate change will play out across much of the continent is deeply uncertain, arguably more so than elsewhere. Plenty about Africa’s changing climate is clear-cut. Its few glaciers are vanishing. The seas along its coasts are rising. Heatwaves are growing longer, more frequent and more intense. A new study by the African Climate & Development Initiative at the University of Cape Town finds that since 2010 hot spells in South Africa have been nearly three times more “extreme”—a measure that combines duration, temperature and the area affected—than in the previous three decades. ALL ELITE athletes face similar challenges. Juggling a busy training schedule with a personal life, for example, or constantly tracking calories and hydration levels. Female athletes have an extra data set to track: their menstrual cycles. In a study of female athletes published in PLOS ONE in 2016, over half of those classified as elite reported that their cycles affected their performance. In a similar study of British track-and-field athletes in 2024, the figure was higher than 75%.
In the absence of clear health guidance, then, it is small wonder that influencers on TikTok have begun offering advice. “Cycle-syncing”, the practice of scheduling everything from workouts to diet around a person’s menstrual cycle, is now ubiquitous. But does it work?
A typical menstrual cycle has two fixed landmarks. One is ovulation, when an egg cell is released from an ovary. The other is the period, when the absence of a fertilised egg causes the uterine lining to shed. The body’s preparation for these events involves significant hormonal swings. Levels of oestrogen, a reproductive hormone, peak around ovulation, while levels of progesterone, another hormone, peak thereafter. Levels of both fall sharply before the period.
The rest of the (typically month-long) cycle is less well-defined. That has not stopped cycle-syncers from embracing a neat division into four distinct phases: menstrual (when bleeding occurs), follicular (when egg-containing follicles grow in the ovary), ovulatory (when an egg is released) and luteal (when empty follicles decay). Advocates claim that energy levels are lowest in the menstrual phase due to low hormone levels and blood loss, before steadily climbing in the follicular phase. Progesterone has been linked to slower digestion and bloating, symptoms which make the luteal phase uncomfortable. The hormonal crash as this phase ends often brings other unwelcome side-effects such as headaches, abdominal cramps and depression.
Advocates for cycle-syncing suggest tailoring activity and diet to these different phases. Workouts should be gentler and iron-rich foods should be prioritised during the menstrual phase, for example. In the follicular phase, the advice is to focus on creative tasks and build up training intensity until ovulation. In the tougher luteal phase, some recommend swapping weight training for yoga and eating fewer sugary foods which can make premenstrual cramps worse.
The structure that cycle-syncing offers women is appealing, but scientists warn that it rests on shaky ground. “There haven’t been rigorous randomised studies,” says Liisa Hantsoo, a women’s-health researcher at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, “so a lot of it is anecdotal.”

Follicular phases, for example, can last anywhere from seven to 21 days. Even a woman’s own cycle is likely to shorten as she ages, or if she switches contraceptive methods.
For those whose daily lives are affected by their cycles, resting when particularly tired is probably wise. But in general, says Dr Hantsoo, “There are no hard and fast rules.” The most sensible advice is to remember that what works for one woman will not necessarily work for another. Tracking your own symptoms to find out what works for you may yield the best results. ■

With messengers taking each item in turn from shop to customer, and each short trip fetching a few cents, it was difficult to turn a profit. So Casey decided to consolidate. He had retailers send all their outgoing items to a central location, where they would be sorted by destination. This made delivery routes more efficient; it also allowed him to charge a premium for a same-day delivery service.
He offered retailers long-term contracts, which saved them from having to spend money on operations (which, in the early 20th century, meant horses and wagons). For Casey, it guaranteed volume and financial surety; and made it harder for rivals to poach his customers.
He was relentless in seeking better ways to work. In the 1920s Casey hired an engineer who had worked at General Motors and Ford to design machinery that would help sort parcels. Trucks were loaded in reverse order of delivery, so that drivers wasted no time scrabbling around for the right item. UPS sent observers armed with stopwatches on deliveries in order to calculate an “ideal performance” for each trip. That benchmark was then used to award bonuses to drivers who made more deliveries than expected. Similar methods are now commonplace at companies such as Amazon. But it was Casey who first embraced automation and an “unapologetic insistence on efficient procedures”.
And competitors “were to be harassed or simply eradicated”. UPS hounded challengers by filing umpteen “complaints, protests and objections”. It flouted antitrust laws by secretly buying up rivals, locking retailers into exclusive contracts and striking deals to carve up markets with competitors. It also persuaded the authorities that “regulations should…be tailored to its needs alone,” winning exemptions from rules that constrained other firms.
In that regard, Casey was again ahead of his time. He was a “demanding taskmaster” with a ruthless, “win-at-all-costs” mentality—the kind that has become de rigueur in Silicon Valley and beyond. The lesson from this book, budding entrepreneurs may feel, is that you should stop at nothing to deliver the goods. ■

He was proud of his labour. From 1975 to 1994, in some of the bleakest and most secret labs in Russia, he and his team had been charged to make substances better, more effective and longer-lasting than anything else available. Two of the most promising, out of the four they synthesised, were his own work. When traces of them turned up he knew them at once by their molecular weight, their spectrometry and their purity. He recognised them as a mother would know her child.
So when in March 2018 a sample was found out in the wider world, Vladimir Uglev didn’t hesitate to claim it as his; and to declare it a “state-level hit”, for Russia was the only possible source. But the circumstances deeply troubled him. His production, the organophosphorus A-234, had been ingested by Sergei Skripal, an elderly man living quietly in retirement in Salisbury, in southern England. Mr Skripal had been a double agent, working for MI6; he had served his jail-time in Russia but was plainly still a target. His daughter Yulia happened to be sitting beside him. In moments he was convulsing and hallucinating, and both fell unconscious, from a mere touch of A-234 on the front-door handle of their house. Four months later and some miles away two innocents, Dawn Sturgess and Charlie Rowley, fell ill after handling an empty perfume bottle that had been thrown away. Sturgess even sprayed it on her wrists. Mr Rowley recovered, but she died. The cause was Novichok, the family of nerve agents to which A-234 belonged. The word meant “newcomer”. Russia’s deadliest secret was now out.
He knew its potency better than anyone. It was ten times more lethal than either VX or Sarin; 50% of 70-kilo individuals would die from two minutes’ exposure. Fundamentally, it played havoc with all the muscular impulses of the body. Three of the four variants his team had made were liquid, with a single drop necessary. The fourth, A-242, was a solid that could be ground into near-invisible powder for dusting, very slightly, on clothes. Though his lab never achieved a more stable binary version, Novichok had a long shelf-life. The fact that it was still effective after four months in the case of “Madam Sturgess” gave him a twinge of satisfaction. He might well have been made that batch with his own hands.
Yet her death also horrified him, and it was not the first. In 1995 Novichok had been smeared on the telephone receiver of Ivan Kivelidi, a banker, and his secretary. Both died. Two deaths occurred of officers engaged in Novichok testing at Shikhany. Most upsetting was the lingering death of a colleague in the lab, Andrei Zheleznyakov. One day, as they worked, he suddenly said: “It’s got me.” A tiny dose of Novichok had spilled into the air. Red and orange circles erupted round him. He was given tea, but vomited it up; he was sent home, but on the way saw a church shining and collapsing. For years he was too ill to work, and he died alone. All these victims remained on Dr Uglev’s conscience.
He himself had a close shave. A tiny splash of solvent in which he was recrystalising Novichok A-242 landed on his hand. He knew the drill: immediately dunked his hand for minutes in hydrochloric acid, then into an alkaline peroxide solution, then rinsed it under the tap. He was shaking, his hands profusely sweating. They kept that habit of sweating for years. He was amazed, too, by how terrified he felt the moment things went wrong.
Yet he was not afraid of speaking out. For what horrified him most was the total denial of the programme by the Putin regime, from Vladimir Vladimirovich down. They said they had never heard of Novichok, or the programme’s formal codename “Foliant”. Obviously the British secret services had staged Salisbury themselves, and then tried to pin it on Russia. True, the chances of tracing the agent’s origin were close to zero. But to deny all knowledge of it was to wipe out his whole career, from university in Moscow to the most hidden research arms of the Soviet Defence Ministry. He disappeared into thin air.
After the Skripal case he therefore made himself fully available to Western journalists and investigations. He tirelessly explained what Novichok was and how it worked, concealing only details of its making that seemed too dangerous to spread. As for the Russian state’s denials, they were a load of shit and total nonsense. He had been slowly disclosing his work since the Soviet Union fell, not least to warn the new satellite states to destroy any Novichok stored with them.
Dissenting came easily. In the 1940s his parents had been sent as punishment to the dismal mining town of Kirovsk beyond the Arctic Circle, which gulag prisoners had been forced to build themselves. That was where he grew up. He had no love either for Russia’s government or for the passivity of most Russians towards their police state. But nothing would change. Cheka, NKVD, KGB, FSB: different names, same goons.
In August 2020 a man on his wavelength, the opposition leader Alexei Navalny, fell violently ill on a flight from Siberia to Moscow. Drink or drugs, said the Kremlin; Novichok, said the West. Dr Uglev instinctively ruled it out, but lay awake night after night worrying. Navalny had slipped into a coma; A-234 didn’t do that. Others around him would have been affected; they weren’t. Yet many good scientists were convinced Novichok was the culprit. It might well have been A-242, even his own batch. If that were to kill Navalny, it would be hard to bear. But it would confirm again that Russia not only had had a cold-war Novichok programme but still, despite pledges to destroy it, a stockpile of the stuff.
Navalny, as it happened, did not die then. He was killed in prison, the world concluded, in 2024, with epibatidine from South American dart-frogs. Mr Uglev’s own death raised suspicions, too. It happened after a heart attack, his son said. But it was not announced for days. If chemistry was involved, he was one of the only scientists who could have known precisely what it was. ■
